his-01.title: What Is History?
explain: This department does not ask you to memorize the history of any one country. Instead, you will learn **how to work with history**: how to read the records that survive, reckon time, think about causes, and compare differing accounts. The villages and people used as examples are all invented.
The **past** is everything that has already happened. It includes every word spoken and every item exchanged in the market yesterday. Most of it vanishes without leaving any trace.
A **source** is a trace the past has left behind. Records, ledgers, letters, objects, buildings, and pictures can all be sources.

**History** is not the past itself. It is an **account** that people create by asking questions about the past and answering them on the basis of surviving sources. That is why history has an author, and why it can be written again when new sources appear or new questions arise.

explain.alt: A diagram of four boxes joined by arrows. The boxes, in order, are: what happened in the past (a dotted box), the sources that remain, the historian's questions and interpretation, and the historical account. A note says most of the past disappears and that perspective enters at the interpretation stage.
explain.caption: From the past to a historical account

explain:
Two kinds of statements are mixed together in a historical account.
- **Fact**: a statement whose truth can be checked against sources. "The ledger records fifty seom of rice."
- **Interpretation**: a statement that links facts together and gives them meaning. "That year was a bumper harvest."

An interpretation may be well supported or poorly supported. Even lining up facts involves choices. The moment a writer picks which of the countless facts to include, the writer's own question is already at work.

examples.title: The Numbers in a Ledger and the Interpretation Above Them
body: Suppose the grain ledger of the fictional village of Solmoe says, "Autumn harvest of 1802: fifty seom of rice." This is a **fact** that you can confirm by looking at the ledger itself.

"That year was a bumper harvest" is an **interpretation**. To call a harvest bumper, you have to compare it with the harvests of other years. If the ledgers for the years before and after show about thirty seom, the interpretation gains strength; if they show forty, the evidence is weaker.

examples.title: A Widely Known General Point
body: In the 1450s, in the mid-fifteenth century, printing with movable type began to spread in Europe, and the speed of producing books increased greatly. This is a widely accepted fact.
But the claim that "therefore people's thinking changed in such-and-such a way" falls within the realm of **interpretation**, where historians debate how much, and by what routes, thinking changed.

his-02.title: Reading Sources
explain:
Sources fall into two broad kinds.
- **Primary source**: something left at or near the time of an event by a person who experienced it or saw it from close up. Diaries, letters, ledgers, and objects of the time.
- **Secondary source**: an account written later on the basis of primary sources and the like. History books, explanatory works, and research papers.

The same document can change category depending on the question. A village storybook written in 1950 is a secondary source when you use it to learn about events of 1802, but a primary source when you use it to study how people in 1950 remembered the past.

explain.alt: A horizontal timeline showing the 1802 event, the writing of a diary in 1802, and the publication of a book in 1950. The diary is linked to a primary source box and the book to a secondary source box, with a note that secondary sources are written later by reading primary sources and the like.
explain.caption: A diary close to the event and a book from a later time

explain:
A primary source is not automatically the truth. That is why we practice **source criticism**, reading sources with careful scrutiny. Here "criticism" does not mean fault-finding; it means examining closely. The basic questions are as follows.
- **Who** wrote it: the author's position and interests
- **When** was it written: how close it is to the event
- **Why** was it written: its purpose, such as record-keeping, persuasion, boasting, or excuse
- **How did the author know**: whether it was seen directly or heard secondhand

A biased source is not thrown away either. As evidence of the author's thinking and position, it can be especially valuable. We simply do not take its words at face value, and we compare it with other sources.

examples.title: A Passage from a Fictional Diary
body: "July 20. The rainy season has dragged on and the river has swollen greatly. Two ferry boats were smashed. The boatman Yun Man-seok says he will repair only one." (Diary of Han Seo-won, village head of Solmoe, 1802)

Who: the village head. When: at the time of the event. How did he know: he was in the village, so he likely saw it directly or heard of it right away. Why: to record village affairs. So it is usable as a primary source.
But "will repair only one" is the head's relay of the boatman's words. It does not tell us the boatman's real thoughts.

When reading it, ask which sources its author saw and whether the author may have wanted to portray the village favorably. Where the book names its sources, you can look them up and compare.

his-03.title: Working with Time
explain: In history, "when" is half of any explanation. The basic tool for handling time is the **timeline**, a line on which events are arranged in chronological order. On a timeline, the tick marks must be evenly spaced for the distances between events to be trusted.

A **century** is a block of 100 years. The 1st century runs from year 1 to year 100, so **there is no year 0.**
- 17th century: 1601-1700
- 18th century: 1701-1800
- 19th century: 1801-1900
- 20th century: 1901-2000

An easy way to find the century: if the year ends in 00, the number before the 00 is the century. Otherwise, add 1 to the first two digits. The year 1745 is 17 + 1 = the 18th century, 1800 is the 18th century, and 1801 is the 19th century. The 1450s belong to the 15th century.

explain.alt: A timeline from 1701 to 1900. The 18th-century section covers 1701-1800 and the 19th-century section covers 1801-1900. The founding of the village school in 1745 and the great flood of 1800 are placed in the 18th century; the completion of the bridge in 1801 and the relocation of the market in 1899 are placed in the 19th century.
explain.caption: A timeline of the fictional village of Solmoe

explain:
**BC** (before the base year) and **AD** (after it) are divided on either side of a reference year. The year after 1 BC is AD 1, and there is no year 0. For BC dates, a larger number means longer ago.
- 300 BC is earlier than 50 BC.
- The 1st century BC runs from 100 BC to 1 BC.

How to find the number of years between two years:
- If both are on the same side (both AD, or both BC), subtract the smaller number from the larger.
- For a year a BC and a year b AD, it is a + b - 1, because there is no year 0.

examples.title: Which Century Is the Year 1800?
body: "1800" contains 18, so it is easy to mistake it for the 19th century. But the 18th century runs from 1701 to 1800, so 1800 is the **last year of the 18th century**.
The 19th century begins only with 1801. This is why, in the timeline, the great flood (1800) and the completion of the bridge (1801) are just one year apart yet fall in different centuries.

his-04.title: Causes and Context
explain:
"Why did it happen?" is the most common question in history. The answer can usually be divided into two layers.
- **Immediate trigger**: the spark just before the event. A single year's bad harvest, a sudden decision.
- **Structural background**: conditions that had built up over a long time. Things that do not change easily, such as population, land, the economy, institutions, and transportation.
By analogy, dry firewood is the structural background and the spark is the immediate trigger. If the firewood is wet, the same spark cannot start a fire.

explain.alt: A diagram read from top to bottom. At the top are three boxes of structural background: narrow farmland and a growing population, the market moving after a new road opened, and long-accumulated grain debts. Below them, next to a plus sign, is the immediate trigger box, the great drought of 1809, and an arrow leads to the result: several households moving to the upper village.
explain.caption: A trigger added to a background produces a result

explain: **Context** is the whole set of conditions of time, place, and society surrounding an event. The same action can mean different things in different contexts. If you ignore context and judge the choices of people of the past only by today's standards, you reach absurd conclusions.

There are common pitfalls when talking about causes.
- **Single-cause fallacy**: explaining a complex event with just one reason.
- **Sequence-equals-cause fallacy**: asserting that because one thing happened first, it must be the cause. Sequence is only a necessary condition for a cause, not evidence of one.
- **Reading backward from the outcome**: saying that because we know the result, it was bound to happen from the start. For the people of the time, many paths were open.

examples.title: The Move out of the Fictional Village of Solmoe
body: Suppose a great drought struck in 1809 and the following year several households moved to the upper village. The explanation "they left because of the drought" is not wrong, but it is shallow.

The farmland was narrow while the population had grown, a new road had moved the market elsewhere, and grain debts had piled up. With this background in place, the trigger of the drought led to the move.
If a neighboring village that went through the same drought did not leave, the next question becomes how the backgrounds of the two villages differed.

his-05.title: The Same Event, Different Accounts
explain:
It is common for writings about the same event to read differently. This is because the person writing chooses four things.
- **Which facts** to include
- **Which words** to use
- **What to emphasize** and what to treat briefly
- **Whose standpoint** to take
**Bias** is a state in which these choices lean to one side. Every account has some point of view. The problem is not the existence of a point of view itself but reading without being aware of it.

explain.alt: The top box states the same event: the ferry fare doubled. It splits into two boxes below. In the boatman's record, the wording is a share of repair costs, the emphasis is the smashed boats, and the omission is the waiting time. In the merchant's record, the wording is suddenly doubled, the emphasis is the increased burden, and the omission is the repair circumstances.
explain.caption: Two records that describe the same event differently

explain:
Clues for recognizing bias are as follows.
- Words loaded with emotion or evaluation ("extorted," "sacred")
- Quoting only one side's sources
- Leaving out the other side's reasons entirely
- Asserting unverifiable matters as certain

Seeing bias does not mean discarding the text. If you know who wrote it from what point of view, and find sources from the opposing point of view and read them together, the event appears more three-dimensional. The goal is not to find writing with no point of view, but to read while recognizing the point of view.

examples.title: Comparing Two Sentences
body: A) "The boatman Yun Man-seok raised the ferry fare to cover the repair costs of the smashed boats."
B) "The boatman Yun Man-seok extorted double the ferry fare overnight."

The two sentences refer to the same thing, but A puts the reason first, while B puts the suddenness and the burden first. "Raised" is a relatively neutral word, while "extorted" is a word that carries the writer's judgment.

his-06.title: Try It Yourself
explain: Now it is time to use everything you have learned. You will read and compare two fictional sources. The two sources continue the story of Solmoe village from the earlier lessons.

**Source A** (diary of Han Seo-won, village head of Solmoe, September 12, 1802)
"Clear. The boatman at the ferry, Yun Man-seok, raised the fare from one doe of rice to two doe. Two boats were smashed in the last rainy season, but only one was repaired, and he says the repairs cost a great deal. The village meeting agreed to the increase. Only a few people voiced complaints."

**Source B** (letter from the merchant Oh Dal-rae of the neighboring market to his business partner, September 14, 1802)
"The fare at the Solmoe ferry has doubled overnight. The village head says everyone agreed at the meeting, but I was never told the date of any meeting. There is only one boat, so we have to wait to cross, and with all our cargo the loss is large for us. There is much talk that the boatman is in-law to the village head."

The following order helps when comparing.
1. Examine the provenance of each source: who, when, why, how did the author know
2. Break each source's claims into sentence-level units
3. Mark where the two sources **agree** and where they **conflict**
4. Speculate about the reasons for the conflict from the authors' positions
5. Write down a provisional conclusion you can draw now and the further sources needed
This is not an assignment with a single fixed answer. It is enough to give evidence and to separate what is confirmed from what is conjecture.

examples.title: Looking at One Line of Comparison
body: Agreement: both sources say the ferry fare doubled. A says "from one doe to two doe" and B says "doubled," so they fit together. Also, A says only one boat was repaired and B says there is only one boat, so these fit together too.

Conflict: A's statement that everyone agreed at the meeting clashes with B's statement that he did not even know the date. Looking at the authors' positions, the village head may have wanted to make the decision look legitimate, and the merchant is the party who suffered a loss.
This much is comparison; to assert that "someone lied" is still premature.

his-07.title: The Ruling Elite and the Office and Land Systems of Ancient Korea and Goryeo
explain: To grasp the character of a premodern state, one must look together at **who monopolizes power and by what system offices and economic bases (rights to collect land tax, suhojo-gwon) are distributed**. The political and social history running from ancient Korea to Goryeo was a process in which a closed status system based on bloodline was reorganized in combination with a bureaucracy and an examination system.

Silla's **골품제 (golpumje, the bone-rank system)** was a strict status system in which the grade of one's bloodline set the upper limit of promotion in the official ranks, and even the size of one's house and the color of one's clothing. Jingol (진골) aristocrats monopolized the highest ranks (ranks 1 to 5) and the posts of chief minister, while the **6두품 (yukdupum, head-rank six)**, who had scholarly ability, ran into the limit known as deuknan (득난, "hard to obtain"): they could not rise above the rank of Achan (아찬, rank 6). Economically, officials were granted **녹읍 (nogeup)**, an allotment from which they could levy not only taxes but also the labor (yeok) of the residents, so the private ruling power of the aristocrats was strong.

explain.alt: A table of changes in the ruling elite and the office and land systems in premodern Korea. It compares the Silla jingol aristocracy with the bone-rank system and nogeup; the early Goryeo munbeol aristocracy with the examination system, eumseo, and jeonsigwa; the late Goryeo gwonmun sejok with the new literati-officials (sinjin sadaebu) and the Gwajeonbeop; and the Joseon yangban sadaebu with the civil, military, and miscellaneous examinations and the Jikjeonbeop.
explain.caption: How the ruling elite reproduced itself moved in step with changes in the selection of officials (eumseo and the examinations) and the distribution of tax-collection rights (jeonsigwa and the Gwajeonbeop).

explain: While integrating the powerful local clans (hojok), Goryeo introduced the **과거제 (gwageoje, the civil service examination system)** (under King Gwangjong, 958) to select officials with Confucian learning. At the same time, through **음서 (eumseo, the hereditary appointment privilege)**, which granted office without examination to the descendants of high officials of rank 5 and above, and through repeated marriage ties with the royal house, it formed a society of **문벌귀족 (munbeol gwijok, aristocratic lineages)**. For land, it operated the **전시과 (jeonsigwa)**, which granted tax-collection rights over jeonji (arable land) and siji (forest for firewood) in graded amounts according to 18 ranks, and gave those of rank 5 and above hereditary **공음전 (gongeumjeon)** to secure the aristocrats' economic base.

Through the military coup of 1170 and the period of Yuan interference, the munbeol aristocracy fell, and the pro-Yuan **권문세족 (gwonmun sejok, powerful families)** annexed great estates, bankrupting state finances. In opposition, the **신진사대부 (sinjin sadaebu, new literati-officials)**, who came from local functionary (hyangri) families and advanced to the center through the Seonggyungwan and the examinations, took Neo-Confucianism as their ideological weapon. After the Wihwado Retreat, they carried out the **과전법 (Gwajeonbeop)** (1391), confiscating the gwonmun sejok's lands and restricting tax-collection land to the Gyeonggi region, thereby preparing the material foundation for founding a new dynasty.

However, the introduction of the examination system in Goryeo must not be overestimated at once as modern meritocracy. In early Goryeo, even those who entered through eumseo could rise to the highest offices, and it was practically very difficult for commoner farmers (yangin) to sit for the examinations, so the system should be understood as a layered one in which aristocratic privilege and bureaucratic operation coexisted.

examples.title: Comparing the Control of Tax-Collection Rights under Jeonsigwa and Gwajeonbeop
body: Goryeo's jeonsigwa granted tax-collection rights over land across the whole country, but at the end of Goryeo the gwonmun sejok expanded their estates in the provinces, producing a situation in which a single plot had several owners.

Step 1: The Gwajeonbeop of 1391 restricted the gwajeon granted to officials, in principle, to the 'Gyeonggi' region around the capital. Step 2: The state collected tax directly from provincial land and secured it as gunjajeon (military supply land).
Interpretation: By tying tax-collection land to Gyeonggi, the state prevented officials from building private power in the provinces, strengthening both state finances and centralization at once.

examples.title: A Structural Contrast between the Silla Yukdupum and the Goryeo New Literati-Officials
body: The Silla yukdupum and the late-Goryeo sinjin sadaebu were both Confucian intellectual strata, but their historical outcomes differed.

Step 1: Silla had no nationwide examination system to replace the bone-rank system, so the yukdupum's path into the highest power within the system was blocked. Step 2: The late-Goryeo sinjin sadaebu secured the institutional ladder of the examination system and the land-reform instrument of the Gwajeonbeop, and led the replacement of the ruling class.
Interpretation: The political rise of an intellectual stratum depended not only on ideology but also on whether it combined a system for selecting officials with the means of economic reform.

his-08.title: Joseon's Neo-Confucian Order, Factional Politics, and the Reform of the Taxation System
explain: Joseon was a **yangban bureaucratic state** that reorganized the bureaucracy and the status system with Neo-Confucianism as its state ideology. In the early period, the **Hungu faction (훈구파)**, which came to power under King Sejo, and the **Sarim faction (사림파)**, based on small and medium landowners in the provinces, clashed over the balance between royal authority and ministerial authority. Despite four literati purges (sahwa, 士禍), the Sarim consolidated their dominance of rural society through **seowon (서원)** (academies for ancestral rites to eminent scholars and for education) and **hyangyak (향약)** (rural self-governing codes), and took control of central politics from the reign of Seonjo in the late sixteenth century.

**Factional politics (붕당정치, bungdang jeongchi)**, which formed after the Sarim came to power along differences in scholarly and political views, was at first a system of coexistence in which factions criticized and checked one another through the power to appoint Ijo jeollang (이조전랑) and through public opinion (gongnon, 公論). In particular, the press activity of the Samsa (the Office of the Inspector-General, the Office of Censors, and the Office of Special Advisors) worked as an institutional device to restrain the arbitrary exercise of royal power and the domination of high ministers.

However, amid the socio-economic upheavals after the two wars (the Imjin War and the Second Manchu Invasion), royal status and Neo-Confucian moral principle clashed sharply through two rounds of **ritual disputes (yesong, 禮訟)**. Beginning with the **hwanguk (換局, regime reversals)** under King Sukjong, the system degenerated into one-party dominance that denied the very existence of rival factions. The **tangpyeong policy (탕평책, policy of impartiality)** of Yeongjo and Jeongjo in the eighteenth century tried to balance personnel appointments around the king, but as the institutional basis supporting royal power weakened, it ended after King Sunjo in the nineteenth century in **sedo politics (세도정치, in-law rule)**, in which a few families related to the royal house monopolized the Border Defense Council (Bibyeonsa) and key offices.

In the economic sphere, the system of land tax-collection rights moved from the Gwajeonbeop through the **Jikjeonbeop (직전법)** (1466), which granted rights only to serving officials, until the granting of tax-collection rights itself disappeared in the mid-sixteenth century and the landlord-tenant system (jiju jeonhoje) became general. Moreover, after the two wars, abandoned fields increased among farmers, and because of the abuse of bangnap (proxy payment), **gongnap (공납, tribute in local products)** became the heaviest burden on farmers. In response, the government enforced the **Daedongbeop (대동법)**, which began in Gyeonggi Province under Gwanghaegun in the seventeenth century and was extended nationwide in the reign of Sukjong (1708). The Daedongbeop converted the local products formerly levied per household to a standard of land area in gyeol (12 du of rice per 1 gyeol), reducing the burden on landless farmers and promoting a commodity-money economy through the gongin (貢人, tribute contractors).

Furthermore, in the reign of Yeongjo, to reduce the abuses of military service, in which adult men had been levied 2 pil of gunpo (군포, military cloth) a year, the **Gyunyeokbeop (균역법)** (1750) was enacted, reducing gunpo to 1 pil, and the reduced revenue was supplemented by collecting gyeoljak (結作, 2 du of rice per 1 gyeol) from landlords, as well as fishery taxes, ship taxes, and seonmu gungwan-po (cloth from lesser military officers). Thus the core direction of the reform of the late-Joseon taxation system was **to shift burdens based on persons (households and adult males) to a basis of land (gyeol)**, but the effect of the reforms was sometimes limited because of the practice of landlords passing the gyeoljak or land tax on to tenant farmers.

examples.title: Calculating the Change in Burden on Farmers and Landlords under the Daedongbeop
body: Suppose that before the reform each household paid the value of local products (equivalent to 20 du of rice) regardless of land ownership, and that after the Daedongbeop was enforced, 12 du of rice was paid per 1 gyeol of land.

Step 1: A tenant-farmer household with 0 gyeol of land goes from the equivalent of 20 du of rice to 0 du of daedong tax, so the burden disappears. Step 2: A great landlord with 10 gyeol goes from 20 du to 10 × 12 = 120 du, so the burden rises sixfold.

Interpretation: The reason the Daedongbeop could spread with farmers' support despite fierce opposition from the yangban landlord class lies in this structure of tax shifting, but the reason it took 100 years to complete was also the landlords' resistance.

examples.title: The Fiscal Compensation Structure of the Gyunyeokbeop
body: If gunpo per commoner adult male (yangin jeongjang) fell from 2 pil to 1 pil, military finances would be halved.
Step 1: To make up the shortfall, gyeoljak of 2 du of rice per 1 gyeol of land was imposed on landlords. Step 2: Some wealthy commoners were given the title seonmu gungwan and levied 1 pil of gunpo.

Interpretation: Within the limits of the status system, which could not directly impose gunpo on the yangban (hopoje, a household-cloth system), it was a compromise that compensated indirectly through a land tax (gyeoljak).

his-09.title: Social Change in Modern and Contemporary Korea: Opening of the Ports, Colonial Rule, Industrialization, and Democratization
explain: Modern and contemporary Korean history was a turbulent process in which the shock of foreign encroachment and colonial rule, imposed from outside, intersected with an internal drive to build an autonomous modern state. After the opening of the ports under the Treaty of Ganghwado (the Korea-Japan Treaty of Amity) in 1876, Joseon went through conflict between enlightenment policies and the movement to defend orthodoxy and reject heterodoxy (wijeong cheoksa), the **Gapsin Coup (갑신정변)** of 1884 (a vision of a modern nation-state, radical reform from above), and the **Donghak Peasant Movement (동학농민운동)** of 1894 (anti-feudal and anti-foreign reform from below).

The **Gabo Reforms (갑오개혁)** of 1894 legally abolished the public and private slave system and the civil service examinations, severing the thousand-year link between the status system and the examination-based bureaucracy. The **Korean Empire (대한제국)**, proclaimed in 1897, pursued land surveys, the issuance of jigye (certificates of modern land ownership), and the promotion of commerce and industry through the Gwangmu Reforms, but leaned toward strengthening absolute imperial power, while the Independence Club held Mass Assemblies (Manmin gongdonghoe) and carried on a constitutional monarchy movement aimed at advancing popular rights and establishing a parliament.

Colonial rule during the Japanese occupation (1910-1945) unfolded as gendarmerie-police rule and the **Land Survey Project (토지조사사업)** in the 1910s, 'cultural rule' and the **Rice Production Increase Plan (산미증식계획)** in the 1920s, and, from the 1930s, the policy of obliterating the Korean nation, the conversion of the peninsula into a logistics base, and total wartime mobilization. The Land Survey Project, through a deadline-based reporting system, increased the Government-General's land-tax revenue and consolidated the colonial landlord system, but reduced many farmers who held customary cultivation rights to fixed-term contract tenants. In opposition, the **March First Movement (3·1 운동)** of 1919 proclaimed the will to national self-determination through nonviolent demonstrations shouting for independence, and the **Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea (대한민국 임시정부)** established as its fruit wrote a democratic republic and the separation of powers into its constitution, becoming the historical origin of today's constitutional order.

After liberation in 1945 and the establishment of the government in 1948, the decisive events that transformed the foundations of Korean society were the **Land Reform (농지개혁)** and the **Korean War (6·25 전쟁)** of 1950. Land reform, carried out on the principle of purchase with compensation and distribution with payment (repayment of 150% of the average annual yield in installments over five years, with land bonds issued to landlords), dismantled the landlord-tenant system that had lasted for hundreds of years and established a system of owner-farmers, creating an equal starting line for the later spread of educational zeal and the formation of the industrial workforce.

From the 1960s to the 1980s, Korea achieved rapid economic growth and urbanization through government-led, export-oriented **industrialization**, but it also bore the shadow of restricted labor rights and political repression under authoritarian rule. Through the April 19 Revolution (1960), the May 18 Democratization Movement (1980), and the **June Democratic Uprising (6월 민주항쟁)** (1987), citizens, students, and workers won a constitutional amendment for direct presidential elections and procedural democracy, thus achieving the dual task of industrialization and democratization.

examples.title: Calculating the Repayment Amount under the 1950 Land Reform
body: Suppose the average yearly harvest of a distributed farm plot is 10 seok of rice, and the repayment condition is 150% of the average harvest, repaid in equal installments over five years.
Step 1: The total amount of rice to be repaid is 10 seok × 1.5 = 15 seok. Step 2: Since it is paid over five years, the amount owed each year is 15 ÷ 5 = 3 seok (30% of the annual harvest).

Interpretation: Compared with tenant rents under Japanese rule, which were 50% or more of the harvest, the farmers' burden fell greatly, and because the land became fully their own after five years, farmers' incentive to produce rose considerably.

Step 1: In the March First Movement of 1919, people of all strata, including students, farmers, workers, and women, took part as agents. Step 2: The Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea in Shanghai proclaimed in Article 1 of its Provisional Constitution that 'the Republic of Korea shall be a democratic republic.'
Interpretation: It is a watershed in constitutional history showing that the seat of sovereignty moved completely from the monarch (emperor) to the people.

his-10.title: The Tang-Song Transition and the Shift in East Asian Tax and Land Systems
explain: In premodern East Asian history, the period from the late eighth to the eleventh century, that is, from the late Tang (唐) to the Song (宋), was the era of the **Tang-Song transition (唐宋變革)**, when the structures of politics, economy, society, and culture changed fundamentally. This view, put forward by the Japanese historian Naito Konan and others, focuses on the watershed at which the medieval order centered on aristocrats gave way to an early modern order centered on imperial autocracy and the scholar-officials (shidafu).

The three pillars of the early-Tang state system were the **equal-field system (均田制, juntian)** (granting a fixed amount of land to adult men and reclaiming it at death), the **zu-yong-diao (租庸調)** (a uniform poll tax of grain, textiles, and labor), and the **fubing system (府兵制)** (a farmer-soldier system in which farmers took turns at military service). All three systems worked on the premise that the state could directly identify and control individual adult men (dingnan, 丁男).

explain.alt: A diagram of four stages in the transformation of tax and service systems of Chinese dynasties. In order: early Tang zu-yong-diao (poll tax on adult men); late Tang Two-Tax Law of 780 (levied twice, in summer and autumn, on household assets and land); late Ming Single Whip Law (land tax and poll tax merged and paid in silver); and Qing Yongzheng Emperor's Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger (poll tax completely folded into the land tax).
explain.caption: East Asian tax history evolved from a system that collected goods and labor on the basis of persons to one that collected money (silver) on the basis of property and land.

explain: However, around the An Lushan Rebellion (755-763) in the mid-eighth century, as great estates (the manor system) of aristocrats and monasteries spread, the land the state could distribute ran out and the equal-field system collapsed. As peasants who had lost their land fled in growing numbers (liumin), the zu-yong-diao, based on counting adult men, and the fubing system were paralyzed together. The **Two-Tax Law (兩稅法)** carried out in 780 at the suggestion of the chief minister Yang Yan changed the paradigm of the tax system. It levied tax on household **assets and land area**, not at the registered home but at the **present place of residence (xianzhudi)**, twice a year in summer (xiashui) and autumn (qiushui), and the military shifted to an **all-volunteer system (募兵制)** that hired professional soldiers.

In the Song period, these changes led to a complete replacement of the ruling class. The Tang aristocratic families that had enjoyed power on the strength of lineage perished amid the wars of the Five Dynasties and Ten Kingdoms, and in the Song, as the examination system was completed with the **palace examination (殿試, dianshi)**, presided over finally by the emperor, the **scholar-officials (士大夫, shidafu)**, a class of landlords and educated men with economic means, advanced into the bureaucracy. The spread of the **tenancy system (佃戶制, dianhu)** (a contractual relationship between landlord and tenant) in the Jiangnan region, the introduction of Champa rice and double cropping, and the circulation of paper money such as the jiaozi and huizi became the material basis of scholar-official society.

One should, however, be wary of the Tang-Song transition thesis equating Song society directly with Western-style modern capitalism. Song scholar-officials were both landlords and bureaucrats subordinate to imperial authority, and tenant farmers likewise could not completely escape economic dependence.

examples.title: Comparing the Tax Burden of Peasants and Great Landlords under Zu-Yong-Diao and the Two-Tax Law
body: Suppose there are a landless tenant household A with one adult man, and a manor landlord household B with one adult man and 100 qing (頃) of land.

Step 1: Under the early-Tang zu-yong-diao, the poll-tax principle means that A and B, with the same number of adult men, bear the same zu, yong, and diao burdens (a regressive structure). Step 2: Under the Two-Tax Law of 780, taxes are levied according to the grade of assets and land area held, so A pays the lowest grade and B the highest.
Interpretation: By accepting great landholding as a fait accompli while shifting the tax base from persons (head counts) to assets (land), the Two-Tax Law achieved both revenue and tax equity.

examples.title: The Political Effects of Song Examination Reform (the Palace Examination, Sealing, and Copying Systems)
body: In the Tang examinations, examiners (zuozhu) and successful candidates (mensheng) formed private cliques, and there was the practice of gongjuan, in which sons of aristocrats made their reputations known beforehand.

Step 1: Emperor Taizu of Song made permanent the 'palace examination,' in which the emperor personally ranks the final results, and introduced the sealing system, which conceals names on answer sheets, and the copying system, which transcribes handwriting. Step 2: All successful candidates became 'the emperor's disciples,' cutting off private ties with examiners.
Interpretation: Strengthening fairness was a device for excluding the influence of hereditary aristocrats and building a bureaucratic system with imperial autocracy at its apex.

his-11.title: The Ming-Qing Gentry, the Silver Economy, and the Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger
explain: The Ming (明) and Qing (淸) periods were an era in which imperial autocracy reached its peak while the **gentry (紳士, shenshi, or xiangshen)**, the ruling class of local society, and a global **silver circulation network** meshed together. Zhu Yuanzhang, the founder of the Ming, tried to bind the countryside to a self-sufficient economy in kind through the lijia system (organizing 110 households into one li) and the Yellow Registers for tax and labor and the Fish-Scale Registers for land, but from the sixteenth century, with the growth of cotton and silk handicrafts in Jiangnan and of nationwide merchant groups (the Huizhou and Shanxi merchants), the commodity-money economy expanded explosively.

The **gentry**, the core ruling class of this period, was a privileged intellectual stratum that included not only examination graduates (jinshi and juren) and retired officials but also **licentiates (生員, shengyuan)**, students enrolled in state schools. Unlike the Song scholar-officials, in the Ming and Qing the competition in the examinations became extremely fierce, and even shengyuan, holders of the lowest degree, often could not advance to central office and remained in the countryside. In return, the state granted the gentry **exemption from corvée labor (yaoyi)** and exemption from light punishments, and the gentry functioned as the pivot of rural rule, assisting local officials' administration and taking charge of maintaining public order, managing irrigation works, and Confucian moral instruction.

Meanwhile, in the latter half of the sixteenth century, silver from the Americas (Potosi mines and others) opened up by Spain and silver from Japan (the Iwami mine and others) flowed in large amounts in exchange for Chinese raw silk and porcelain, advancing the **silver standardization** of the Chinese economy. Accordingly, during the Wanli Emperor's reign of the Ming, the chief minister Zhang Juzheng extended nationwide the **Single Whip Law (一條鞭法)**, which bundled the complicated land tax, poll tax (dingshui), and miscellaneous labor services into one and **collected them all in silver** according to land area and the number of adult men.

Even in the Qing, the practice of hiding adult men (dingnan) to avoid taxes continued among the gentry and great landlords, so the Kangxi Emperor proclaimed in 1712 **the Shengshi zisheng rending, yong bu jia fu (盛世滋生人丁 永不加賦, no additional levy on newly increased population)**, which permanently froze the total poll tax on the basis of the number of adult men at that time. Subsequently, the Yongzheng Emperor completed the **Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger (地丁銀制, diding yin)**, which folded the fixed poll tax (dingshui) entirely into the land tax (dishui) and collected it in silver solely according to the amount of land held.

With the enforcement of the Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger, the 'absorption of the poll tax into the land tax' that began with the Two-Tax Law of the late Tang was completed after about 950 years. Landless peasants were entirely freed of the poll tax burden, and as the reason to hide household registers disappeared, the Qing's official population rose sharply from about 100 million in the early eighteenth century to over 400 million in the mid-nineteenth century, and the movement of surplus labor into commerce and industry and newly reclaimed lands became active.

examples.title: Comparing Tax Amounts under the Single Whip Law and the Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger
body: Suppose that in a certain region, under the Single Whip Law system, 2 qian of silver was collected as land tax per mu (畝) of land and 1 qian of silver per adult man as poll tax, and that when it was changed to the Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger, the poll tax was folded into the land tax at 20% (a total of 2.4 qian per mu).

Step 1: A poor-peasant household with 0 mu of land and 3 adult men paid 3 qian of silver under the Single Whip Law, but pays 0 qian of silver under the Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger. Step 2: A landlord household with 50 mu of land and 2 adult men paid (50×2)+(2×1)=102 qian under the Single Whip Law, but pays 50×2.4=120 qian under the Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger.

Interpretation: The Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger completely integrated the poll tax into the land tax, eliminated the tax burden on landless poor peasants, and enforced taxation in proportion to landholding.

examples.title: The Link between the Atlantic-Pacific Silver Trade and the Ming-Qing Tax Systems
body: For farmers to pay taxes in silver (under the Single Whip Law and the Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger), they must sell farm products on the market to obtain silver.

Step 1: China's domestic silver production alone could not meet the nationwide demand for tax payment in silver. Step 2: Through the Manila galleon trade (American silver) and Japanese silver, silver flowed in as payment for exports of Chinese silk and porcelain, supplying the currency in which taxes circulated.

Interpretation: When the inflow of silver dropped sharply in the mid-seventeenth century because of abnormal weather and disruptions in foreign trade, the price of silver soared (grain prices collapsed), so farmers' real tax burden rose sharply, and this became one of the economic backgrounds of the fall of the Ming.

his-12.title: The Dissolution of the East Asian Tribute-Investiture Order and the Transition to Modern Nation-States
explain: The basic framework of the premodern East Asian international order combined the **tribute-investiture system (朝貢冊封體制)**, in which neighboring states sent envoys and gifts to a Chinese dynasty and received investiture, with the Ming and Qing sea bans (haijin) and the seclusion (sakoku) of Japan's Edo shogunate (restricted trade at Dejima in Nagasaki). Unlike the modern Western treaty system of sovereign equality, it was a distinctive international society that combined a hierarchical ritual order with official trade (such as tally trade).

In the mid-nineteenth century, the military advance of the Western industrial-capitalist powers shook this order to its roots. To offset its trade deficit with the Qing (the outflow of silver caused by imports of tea and silk), Britain smuggled Indian opium, and using the Qing's crackdown on opium as a pretext, it started the **First Opium War** (1840-1842). The **Treaty of Nanjing** (1842) concluded as a result ceded Hong Kong, opened five ports including Guangzhou, and abolished the Cohong (the monopoly merchant guild), while stipulating **consular jurisdiction (extraterritoriality)**, **conventional tariffs**, and **most-favored-nation treatment**, and became the prototype of the East Asian unequal treaty system.

The responses of China, Korea, and Japan to the Western shock diverged according to their internal political and social structures. In the Qing, Han Chinese officials such as Zeng Guofan and Li Hongzhang, who had suppressed Hong Xiuquan's **Taiping Rebellion** (1851-1864, which advocated the Tianchao tianmu system of equal land distribution), carried out the **Self-Strengthening Movement** under the banner of 'Chinese learning as the essence, Western learning for practical use' (中體西用: keep the traditional Chinese system and adopt only Western military technology), but it was frustrated by defeat in the Sino-Japanese War (1894-1895), having left the autocratic monarchy and bureaucratic corruption untouched. Then, through the **Hundred Days' Reform** of Kang Youwei and Liang Qichao (1898, aiming at constitutional monarchy), the **Xinhai Revolution** (1911) based on Sun Yat-sen's Three Principles of the People brought down two thousand years of imperial rule and established the Republic of China, the first republic in Asia.

Japan, by contrast, concluded the Convention of Kanagawa (1854) and the Treaty of Amity and Commerce (1858) with the United States after Commodore Perry's show of force, and then lower-ranking samurai of the southwestern powerful domains such as Satsuma and Choshu overthrew the shogunate and carried out the **Meiji Restoration** (1868), establishing a centralized state centered on the emperor. The Meiji government rapidly laid the foundations of a modern nation-state through the **abolition of the domains and establishment of prefectures (haihan chiken)**, the abolition of the status system (equality of the four classes), the **land-tax reform (chiso kaisei)** (collecting 3% of land value in cash), and conscription, and under pressure from the Freedom and People's Rights Movement it enacted the **Constitution of the Empire of Japan** (1889), Asia's first modern constitution.

However, Japan's modernization remained a facade constitutionalism that stipulated the emperor's sacred inviolability and the independence of the supreme military command, and it led directly to imperialist expansion: encroaching on Korea and fighting the Sino-Japanese and Russo-Japanese Wars. Therefore, the modern transition of East Asia must be analyzed not as a simple dichotomy of 'success and failure of Westernization' but in its full dimension: how modern reform, imperialist aggression, and anti-imperialist national movements became intertwined in the process by which the tribute order was replaced by a system of sovereignty and treaties.

examples.title: Calculating Tax under Japan's Land-Tax Reform (1873) and the Stabilization of State Finances
body: In the Edo period, 40-50% of the harvest was collected in rice in kind, so shogunate finances swung widely with good or bad harvests and fluctuations in the rice price. The land-tax reform of 1873 assessed land value (chika) and collected 3% of it in cash from landowners.
Step 1: The annual land tax on a field assessed at 200 yen is 200 × 0.03 = 6 yen. Step 2: Whether the harvest is good or bad, the government collects a fixed 6 yen in cash every year.

Interpretation: The state secured a modern fiscal system in which budgets could be planned and raised funds for promoting industry, but farmers were left to bear in full the risks of bad harvests and plunging rice prices.

examples.title: How the Three Poisonous Clauses of the Unequal Treaties Worked
body: The Treaty of Nanjing (and supplementary treaties), the Treaty of Amity and Commerce with the United States, and the Treaty of Ganghwado all contained common unequal mechanisms.

Step 1: Consular jurisdiction had foreign nationals' crimes in treaty ports tried by their own consuls, infringing judicial sovereignty. Step 2: Conventional tariffs fixed tariff rates low by agreement with the other country, preventing the protection of domestic infant industries, and most-favored-nation treatment automatically extended any privilege granted to other countries.
Interpretation: Beyond military defeat, these three clauses legally constrained the economic and judicial independence of East Asian states.

his-13.title: Ancient Western Citizen Communities and the Growth of Medieval Feudalism and Towns
explain: The two pillars of premodern Western history are the **citizen communities (polis and the Roman Republic)** of the ancient Mediterranean world and **feudalism and the manorial system** of medieval Europe. Ancient Athenian democracy, through Cleisthenes' reorganization of the tribes and, in Pericles' time, pay for officeholders, the use of the lot, and ostracism, brought to flower a **direct democracy** in which adult male citizens took part directly in the assembly and the jury courts. But this citizenship operated only on a privileged community that excluded women, foreigners (metoikoi), and the many slaves who did the productive labor.

After overthrowing the monarchy, Rome developed a **republic** that dispersed power among consuls (administrative and military), the Senate (an assembly of aristocrats), and the popular assemblies. The plebeians, on the strength of their military contribution as heavy infantry, waged the struggle of the orders, including the secession of the plebs, and won the office of **tribune of the plebs**, the **Twelve Tables** (written law), and the Hortensian law (which recognized plebiscites as binding on the whole state). But as conquered territories widened after the Punic Wars, slave-worked great estates (latifundia) spread and independent farmers declined, and after the failed reforms of the Gracchi brothers and civil wars among warlords, Rome moved to Augustus's **principate (a de facto empire)**.

Amid the fall of the Western Roman Empire, the migrations of Germanic peoples, and the invasions of Muslims, Normans, and Magyars in the eighth and ninth centuries, Western Europe formed not a centralized state but a distinctive decentralized order called **feudalism**. Its political side, the **lord-vassal relationship**, was one in which lord and vassal entered a reciprocal contract: the lord granted a fief and the vassal offered military service and loyalty. Because a vassal exercised **immunity (judicial and taxing authority)** within his own fief, free from the lord's interference, the lord-vassal relationship, unlike China's commandery-county system, had a contractual and decentralized character.

In the **manorial system (manorialism)**, the economic foundation, most peasants were **serfs**. Unlike ancient slaves, serfs were bound by status to the lord's land and had no freedom to move, and bore labor services, dues, and marriage and death taxes, yet they formed their own households and held their own share of cultivated land, which gave them a minimal basis for subsistence.

From the eleventh century, as the three-field system (a rotation dividing land into spring-crop, autumn-crop, and fallow fields) and the spread of the heavy wheeled plow raised agricultural productivity, long-distance trade and **medieval towns** revived. Merchants and craftsmen formed guilds, obtained charters from lords, and won self-government and the freeing of serfs ('town air makes one free'). Then, when the **Black Death (plague)** of the fourteenth century caused population to plummet, the value of labor soared and lords converted labor services into money rents, and serfdom and the manorial system in Western Europe set out on the path to dissolution.

examples.title: Moving from the Two-Field to the Three-Field System and Calculating the Increase in Cultivated Area
body: Suppose a manor with 120 hectares of farmland changed its farming method from the two-field system (1/2 fallow) to the three-field system (1/3 fallow) to restore soil fertility.

Step 1: Under the two-field system, the area actually sown each year is 120 × (1/2) = 60 hectares. Step 2: Under the three-field system, the area sown each year (spring-crop plus autumn-crop fields) is 120 × (2/3) = 80 hectares.

Interpretation: Even with the total land area unchanged, the actually cultivated area increases by 33.3%, from 60 to 80 hectares; spreading the harvests across spring and autumn reduces the risk of famine and makes it possible to grow oats as horse fodder.

examples.title: Comparing the Western European Lord-Vassal System with Chinese Lords and Commanderies and Counties
body: Let us analyze the Western European feudal maxim 'My vassal's vassal is not my vassal.'

Interpretation: This tradition of reciprocal contract became the historical soil of the Magna Carta of 1215, in which English nobles had King John confirm the right of consent to taxation and due process.

his-14.title: The Atlantic Civic Revolutions and the Formation of the Modern Constitutional and Republican Order
explain: The **Atlantic civic revolutions**, which occurred in succession in England, the North American colonies, and France from the late seventeenth to the late eighteenth century, were a vast political transformation that brought down the Ancien Régime, founded on the divine right of kings and the privileges of the status order, and established a modern constitutional order based on **natural rights, the social contract, popular sovereignty, and the separation of powers**.

In England, the Puritan Revolution (1642-1649) arose against the despotic rule of Charles I of the Stuart dynasty and his taxation without parliamentary consent, passing through an experiment in republican government; then Parliament, resisting the despotism of James II, replaced the monarch without bloodshed in the **Glorious Revolution** (1688) and secured acceptance of the **Bill of Rights** (1689). With this, the **constitutional monarchy**, in which 'the king reigns but does not rule,' and the tradition of parliamentary sovereignty were established.

explain.alt: A comparison table of the course and constitutional principles of the three great Atlantic civic revolutions. It compares the English Revolution (Bill of Rights, constitutional monarchy), the American Revolution (Declaration of Independence and federal Constitution, federal republic and separation of powers), and the French Revolution (Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, the republican experiment, the distinction between active and passive citizens) in terms of the triggering occasion, key documents, political system, and limits of suffrage.
explain.caption: The three great civic revolutions declared universal human rights, but began with the historical limitation that early suffrage was confined to propertied white men.

explain: The thirteen North American colonies, who resisted British mercantilist taxation (the Stamp Act and the tea duty) with 'no taxation without representation,' issued the **Declaration of Independence** in 1776, which proclaimed Locke's social contract theory and the right of resistance, and won the war of independence. The **Constitution of the United States of 1787**, enacted next, as the world's first written constitution, institutionalized **federalism**, combining the self-government of the states with a central government, and a strict **separation of powers** (checks and balances) among legislative, judicial, and executive branches, proving that a democratic republic could work even in a large country.

The **French Revolution**, which broke out in 1789, exploded from the contradictions and fiscal crisis of the Ancien Régime, in which the First Estate (clergy) and the Second Estate (nobility) enjoyed tax exemptions while the Third Estate (bourgeoisie, peasants, and townspeople), 98% of the population, bore the taxes alone. The **Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen** (1789), issued after the National Assembly's Tennis Court Oath and the storming of the Bastille, proclaimed liberty, equality, popular sovereignty, and the inviolability of property as universal principles. The revolution then unfolded breathlessly from a constitutional monarchy (the Constitution of 1791) through the execution of Louis XVI, the radical republic and Reign of Terror of the Jacobins (Robespierre), and the Directory, to Napoleon's Consulate and Empire, and through the **Napoleonic Code** (civil code, 1804), equality before the law and private property rights spread across Europe.

But the substance of the 'universal citizen' proclaimed by the early civic revolutions was limited to **propertied white men**. The French Constitution of 1791 divided citizens into 'active citizens,' who had the right to vote according to the amount of tax they paid, and 'passive citizens,' who did not, and women (as Olympe de Gouges's 'Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen' pointed out) and colonial slaves (the background of the Haitian Revolution) were excluded. This very gap between proclaimed ideals and reality became a powerful driving force of the suffrage-expansion movements of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

examples.title: The Political Maneuvering over the Voting Method of the French Estates-General in 1789
body: The delegates to the Estates-General convened in 1789 numbered about 300 for the First Estate (clergy), about 300 for the Second Estate (nobility), and about 600 for the Third Estate (commoners).

Step 1: If voting is 'by estate (one vote per estate)' as in Ancien Régime practice, the privileged estates (First plus Second) always win, 2 to 1. Step 2: If voting is 'by head (one vote per delegate)' as the Third Estate demanded, the Third Estate (600 votes), joined by some liberal-minded nobles and lower clergy, can take a majority (601 votes or more).

Interpretation: The dispute over the voting method was not a mere matter of procedure but a struggle over sovereignty, deciding whether a 'representative body of estates' would become a 'modern parliament (the National Assembly) representing the whole nation.'

examples.title: Locke's Theory of the Right of Resistance and the Logical Structure of the American Declaration of Independence
body: How did the American Declaration of Independence (1776) justify rebellion against the British king George III?

Step 1 (major premise): All people have the natural rights of life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness, and governments are instituted by the consent of the governed to secure these rights. Step 2 (minor premise and conclusion): When a government destroys this purpose, the people have the right to alter or abolish it (the right of resistance); the British king committed tyranny such as taxation without representation, so independence is justified.
Interpretation: By combining natural law and social contract theory in the form of a syllogism, it elevated the colonial rebellion into an act of defending universal human rights.

his-15.title: The Industrial Revolution, the Capitalist World-System, and Imperialism
explain: The **Industrial Revolution**, which began in Britain in the late eighteenth century, was a world-historical transformation that shifted humanity's main energy source from biological muscle power and wood to **fossil fuel (coal) and the steam engine**, and shifted the organization of production from domestic handicraft and manufactories (factory-style handicraft) to the **machine-based large factory (the factory system)**.

A combination of conditions explains why the Industrial Revolution occurred first in Britain. These included the protection of property rights and political stability after the Glorious Revolution; gains in agricultural productivity through the second **enclosure movement** (fencing in of farmland) and the conversion of the surplus rural population into urban labor; abundant deposits of **coal and iron ore**; and capital accumulated through colonial trade together with vast overseas markets (in particular the demand for cotton spinning and weaving to replace Indian cotton cloth). James Watt's improvement of the steam engine, the invention of the spinning machine and power loom, and Stephenson's steam locomotive and the building of railway networks compressed the space and time of production and transport.

Industrialization fundamentally reorganized the social class structure. The **industrial capitalists (the bourgeoisie)**, who owned the means of production (factories and machines), and the **wage workers (the proletariat)**, who sold only their labor power for wages, emerged as the core classes. Long working hours, low-paid labor of children and women, and poor sanitation in early industrial cities gave rise to what came to be called the 'social question.' Workers went beyond machine-breaking (the Luddites) to forming trade unions and movements to extend suffrage (the British **Chartist movement**, 1838-1848), and Marx and Engels, in the *Communist Manifesto* (1848), presented scientific socialism analyzing the inherent contradictions of capitalism and class struggle.

As the **Second Industrial Revolution**, centered on electricity, chemicals, the internal combustion engine, and steel, spread to Germany, the United States, and elsewhere in the late nineteenth century, monopoly capitalism arose, combining giant monopoly capital and finance capital. The powers' competition to secure outlets for overproduced goods and surplus capital from their home markets, and cheap raw materials (rubber, oil, minerals), rushed toward the **New Imperialism (1870-1914)**, in which Asia and Africa were directly partitioned and occupied as colonies with military force at the fore.

At the Berlin Conference of 1884-1885, the powers drew boundary lines irrespective of the wishes of Africans and partitioned more than 90% of the African continent (with clashes such as Britain's north-south policy against France's east-west policy), and justified aggression with eugenics, **social Darwinism** (an ideology that unjustly applied 'survival of the fittest' to human society and races), and the discourse of the 'white man's burden.' This imperialist scramble for colonies and the secret alliance systems of the Triple Alliance and Triple Entente finally brought about the catastrophe of total war in **World War I** in 1914.

examples.title: Calculating the Increase in Productivity per Unit of Labor Time from Mechanized Spinning
body: Suppose spinning 100 pounds of cotton yarn with a hand spinning wheel took 50,000 labor hours, but after the introduction of the spinning mule and the steam engine, the same amount took 250 labor hours.
Step 1: The required labor time fell from 50,000 hours to 250 hours. Step 2: The multiple of labor productivity is 50,000 ÷ 250 = 200 times.
Interpretation: With this overwhelming drop in unit cost, British machine-made cotton cloth in turn destroyed India's traditional handicraft cotton industry and dominated the world market.

body: Why did the European powers, who cried for free trade in the early nineteenth century, throw themselves into high tariffs and exclusive partition of colonial territory in the late nineteenth century?

Step 2: When concessions in railways and mines and monopoly markets became necessary to invest surplus capital at high returns, state military power was mobilized.
Interpretation: Imperialism was not simply a product of national glory but a structural expansion mechanism of the monopoly-capitalist stage.

his-16.title: Ranke's Positivist Historiography and the Foundations of External and Internal Source Criticism
explain: History established itself as an independent modern discipline, freed from being a branch of literature or moral philosophy, with the nineteenth-century German historian **Leopold von Ranke**. Ranke declared that the historian's task is not to judge the past or to draw lessons for the future, but only to show, on the basis of rigorous sources, **'how it actually was' (wie es eigentlich gewesen)**.

The core methodology of Ranke's historiography was strict **source criticism (Quellenkritik)** combined with the university **seminar (Seminar)** system. He gave first priority to **primary sources**, such as diplomatic documents, official government papers, and letters written at the time of the event, over secondary works or memoirs compiled later. Source criticism proceeds in two broad stages.

First, **external criticism (authenticity criticism)** is the work of determining the physical and formal authenticity of a source. By checking the material of the paper and ink, the handwriting, the document formats of contemporary offices, and the vocabulary and era names used, one distinguishes whether a document is a **forgery** fabricated later or a genuine contemporary original (or a copy derived from one). A classic example is the *Donation of Constantine*, which the medieval papacy used as a basis for secular territorial rule; the fifteenth-century humanist Lorenzo Valla demonstrated that it was an eighth-century forgery by pointing to anachronisms in its Latin vocabulary.

Second, **internal criticism (credibility criticism)** is the work, after a source has been confirmed as genuine, of judging **how trustworthy the content** written in it is. It analyzes whether the author was in a position to witness the events directly, whether there was a motive to cover up his own political errors or inflate his achievements, and whether the prejudices or censorship of the time intervened. Accuracy in internal criticism increases when one cross-checks sources from the opposing camp recording the same event or diplomatic documents from third countries.

But Ranke's positivist historiography also had clear limits. First, by treating as absolute the official diplomatic and political documents of state archives, it narrowed history to **political history (event history) centered on states, monarchs, diplomats, and wars**, and left out of view the lives of commoners, women, and colonial subjects who left no writing, and socioeconomic structures. Second, it overlooked that the historian's present perspective and value judgments are already at work the moment he selects and arranges sources, and so it remained at a naive belief in so-called 'presuppositionless objectivity.' From reflection on these limits arose the twentieth-century Annales school, Marxist historiography, and the historical theory of E. H. Carr.

examples.title: Distinguishing Actual Applications of External and Internal Criticism
body: Suppose a 'handwritten campaign diary' said to have been left by the commander of a certain battle in the mid-seventeenth century is newly discovered.

Step 1 (external criticism): Examine the radiocarbon date of the hanji (paper) used in the diary, the style of the script, and whether place names in the text are names that came after the nineteenth-century reorganization of administrative districts. If nineteenth-century place names appear, it is a later forgery. Step 2 (internal criticism): If it is confirmed as a genuine seventeenth-century document, check against the other side's military ledgers whether the commander inflated the enemy's troop numbers tenfold in order to shift responsibility for the defeat onto his subordinates.
Interpretation: External criticism asks 'is this document really from that time?'; internal criticism asks 'may the words written in a genuine document be believed as they stand?'

examples.title: The Blind Spots Produced by the 'Primary-Source Bias' of Ranke's Historiography
body: Suppose a nineteenth-century epidemic in an urban slum is described using only the police department's official report (a primary official document).

Step 1: The police report records the slum only as 'filthy and a controlled area at risk of riot.' Step 2: Unless one also looks at the oral accounts of slum residents, household account books, medical practices, and housing-rent ledgers, the poor will be portrayed only as passive objects.
Interpretation: Even if an official document is a genuine primary source, it is a biased record bearing 'the state's gaze,' so cross-checking with unofficial and material sources is essential.

his-17.title: Braudel's Three Layers of Time in the Annales School and Marxist Historiography
explain: The two great currents that broke through the limits of Rankean political and diplomatic event history in the first half of the twentieth century and widened the horizons of historical study were the French **Annales School** and **Marxist historiography**. The journal *Annales (Annals of Economic and Social History)*, founded in 1929 by Marc Bloch and Lucien Febvre, advocated a **total history (Histoire totale)** encompassing geography, climate, population, prices, and collective mentalities (Mentalité), going beyond the surface of political events, and interdisciplinary cooperation with neighboring social sciences.

**Fernand Braudel**, representing the second generation of the Annales school, argued in his masterwork *The Mediterranean and the Mediterranean World in the Age of Philip II* (1949) that historical time does not flow at a single speed, and presented a model of **three layers of time (a threefold division)**.

explain.alt: A diagram of Braudel's three layers of time in the Annales school and the flow of modern historiography. On the left are layer 1, event history (short time, individuals, battles and treaties); layer 2, conjunctural history (medium time, socioeconomic, price and population cycles); and layer 3, the longue durée (structures, geography, ecology, mentalities, a deep foundation on the scale of centuries). On the right is summarized the shift of the central axis from Rankean positivist history to the Annales and Marxism, microhistory and the new cultural history, and global history.
explain.caption: Braudel compared political events to 'foam' on a deep sea and drew attention to the structures of the longue durée.

explain: Braudel's first layer is the **longue durée (structural time)**: the geographic and ecological environment and the systems of agriculture and sea routes that barely change over centuries or more. The second layer is **conjunctural history (Conjoncture, medium-term socioeconomic time)**: price waves, population changes, and wage trends that rise and fall in cycles of 10 to 50 years. The third layer is **event history (Histoire événementielle, short-term individual time)**: battles, treaties, and changes of kings that occur on a scale of a day or a few months. Braudel compared the event history that traditional historiography clung to to 'foam' that glitters on deep currents and then vanishes, and held that one must clarify the deep structures of the longue durée that define the range of possibility for events.

Meanwhile, **Marxist historiography** (historical materialism) found the fundamental driving force of social change in the **mode of production (the base)**, the combination of productive forces and relations of production, and in **class struggle**. In particular, New Left historians in Britain such as Eric Hobsbawm and E. P. Thompson went beyond economic determinism and pioneered **'history from below.'** In *The Making of the English Working Class* (1963), Thompson showed that class is not a statistical category but a historical relationship that ordinary people make for themselves through their cultural experiences and struggles over the moral economy.

However, the structure-centered narration of the Annales school and the macro models of classical Marxism ran the risk (structural determinism) of **reducing human beings to passive puppets of vast geographic and economic structures**, erasing individuals' agency in choosing and the role of contingency. Out of reflection on this, microhistory and the new cultural history emerged from the 1970s onward.

examples.title: Analyzing the Battle of Lepanto in 1571 through Braudel's Three Layers
body: Let us divide the Battle of Lepanto in 1571, in which the Holy League fleet centered on Spain met the Ottoman fleet, into three time layers.

Step 1 (event history, short term): the battle tactics over the single day of October 7, 1571, and the decisions of the commander Don John. Step 2 (conjunctural history, medium term): the Mediterranean price revolution caused by the inflow of American silver in the late sixteenth century, and the trends in the finances and shipbuilding capacity of the two empires.

Step 3 (longue durée, structure): the ecological and geographic limits of the Mediterranean, where, because of the winter north winds and narrow straits, galley fleets could maneuver along the coastline only in spring and summer. Interpretation: the reason Spain could not permanently control the eastern Mediterranean despite the naval victory lay in the geographic structure of the longue durée and the medium-term fiscal conjuncture.

examples.title: Applying E. P. Thompson's Concept of the 'Moral Economy'
body: Can the food riots of eighteenth-century Britain be seen simply as 'instinctive looting by a hungry crowd'?

Step 1: From Thompson's analysis of sources, the crowd did not simply steal bread; it prevented merchants' hoarding, forced the sale of bread at the customary 'fair price,' and then handed the proceeds to the merchants. Step 2: This was conscious resistance based on a traditional norm (the moral economy) that the community's right to subsist takes precedence over free-market profit.
Interpretation: History from below restores rational norms and agency in the actions of nameless ordinary people.

his-18.title: Microhistory, the New Cultural History, and the Transnational Global Perspective
explain: From the 1970s and 1980s, historical study rebelled against vast socioeconomic statistics and structural determinism and opened new breakthroughs with **microhistory (Microhistory)**, which narrows the magnification of the observing microscope to a single village or individual, and the **new cultural history (New Cultural History)**, which analyzes symbols, rituals, and linguistic discourse.

**Microhistory**, led by Carlo Ginzburg of Italy and others, **deliberately reduces the scale (Scale) of observation**. This is because contradictions and fissures that are buried in the average values of macro statistics come to light only when one traces the life of a single person or an event in a small village closely. In *The Cheese and the Worms* (1976), Ginzburg closely read the Inquisition records of the sixteenth-century Italian miller Menocchio and showed that the peasant had not passively accepted elite doctrine but had combined oral culture with reading to create his own cosmology. A clue that, through seemingly deviant records from the periphery, lets us trace back the silent culture of the majority of that time is called the **'exceptional normal' (Exceptional Normal)**.

The **new cultural history** drew on the anthropologist Clifford Geertz's **'thick description' (Thick Description, an interpretation that reads layer upon layer the cultural context and symbolic system behind actions)** and Michel Foucault's theories of discourse and power. In *The Great Cat Massacre* (1984), Robert Darnton analyzed the strange incident in which eighteenth-century Parisian printers' apprentices killed their master and mistress's cats and burst into laughter, and showed that the very point of strangeness at which we fail to understand the jokes of people of that time is the key to entering the mentalities and symbolic world of the past.

Furthermore, Hayden White, a theorist of the postmodernist current, argued in *Metahistory* that historical writing is also a linguistic construct that weaves sources into a plot (emplotment), and so is no different from literary narrative (the **linguistic turn, Linguistic Turn**). This prompted reflection on the historian's narrative strategies, but if history is equated with pure fiction (the novel), it can fall into an extreme relativism that denies even the reality of historical facts such as the Holocaust or colonial crimes. Therefore contemporary historical study maintains a balance that **acknowledges the 'constructedness of narrative' while preserving the 'veto power of sources' (the power to reject fictional interpretations that the sources do not permit).**

In the twenty-first century, historical study has been expanding beyond the prison of 'national history' (history in the unit of the modern nation-state), taken for granted since the nineteenth century, into **transnational history (Transnational History)** and **global history (Global History)**. Just as Kenneth Pomeranz, in *The Great Divergence*, compared the economic levels of Britain and China's Jiangnan on an equal footing up to the eighteenth century and found the causes of the divergence in the location of coal and the presence or absence of American colonies, global history leaves Eurocentrism behind and traces the interconnectedness of global networks of exchange, epidemics, ecology, and migration.

examples.title: Microhistory's 'Reduced Scale' and How to Read Inquisition Sources
body: Sixteenth-century peasants left no writing, so how did Ginzburg recover the thought of the peasant Menocchio?

Step 1: The trial transcript written by the interrogator (the inquisitor) is a hostile record by the powerful, but it contains a verbatim record of the defendant's statements. Step 2: He filters out the interrogator's leading questions and attends to Menocchio's odd metaphor, which baffled the interrogator ('the world arose out of chaos as worms appear in cheese').
Interpretation: By 'reading against the grain' the official document of the oppressor (the trial record), it shows the essence of microhistory: fishing out the voice of the oppressed.

examples.title: Comparing the National-History and Global-History Perspectives: The Crisis of the Seventeenth Century
body: How should we explain the fall of the Ming dynasty (1644), the English Puritan Revolution (1642), and Joseon's famine (the Great Famine of the Gyeongsin years) in the mid-seventeenth century?

Step 1 (national history): Each is explained separately by the corruption of each country's dynasty or the misrule of its monarch. Step 2 (global history): It is demonstrated by cross-checking that harvest failures from the temperature drop of the 'Little Ice Age' that struck the whole Northern Hemisphere, and the contraction of the Atlantic-Pacific silver circulation network, triggered simultaneous fiscal and ecological crises across Eurasia.
Interpretation: When one looks at the networks of climate and trade beyond national borders, macro-level causation appears that sources within individual states alone did not reveal.
