his-19.title: Bachelor's Capstone I: Cross-Criticism of Multiple Sources and Quantitative and Structural Inference
explain: The first comprehensive task of the history major is to **cross-criticize, externally and internally, multiple sources that contradict one another or are biased (official records, personal diaries, trial records, quantitative ledgers)**, and to combine the structural models learned in Korean, East Asian, Western, and historiographical studies to infer historical causation. Now let us examine four sources on a tax-refusal incident (a refusal to pay taxes) that occurred in the fictional coastal county of 'Cheongpo (淸浦縣)' in the mid-eighteenth century.

**[Source A: Report to the central government by the magistrate of Cheongpo County (genuine official document, 1755)]** 'This autumn, under the pretext of a poor harvest, several hundred vagrants of unruly character came crowding to the county office and caused a disturbance, but this official sternly admonished them and had them disperse at once, and the county's collection of taxes is being carried out fairly according to the statutes.' / **[Source B: Diary of Kim, a rural gentry landlord (genuine handwritten copy, 1755)]** 'The clerks of the county office, while collecting gyeoljak and daedongmi, extorted in addition to the statutory standard of 14 du per gyeol (12 du of daedongmi plus 2 du of gyeoljak) a further 7 du per gyeol under the names of "inju rice" and fees, and passed this on to the tenants; so the tenants took up farm tools, occupied the market, and blocked the gates of the county office for three days.'

**[Source C: Peasant manifesto found in the twentieth century (dated with the Western calendar year 1755 instead of an era name, on chemical-pulp paper)]** 'Let us overthrow all feudal landlordism and build a proletarian self-governing republic!' / **[Source D: Cheongpo County office accounting ledger and market rice-price time series (1750-1755)]** In 1755 the county's total farmland was 1,000 gyeol, and the statutory levy was 14,000 du (14 du per gyeol), but the amount actually received into the county storehouse is recorded as 21,000 du. In the same year, a cold spell cut the rice harvest to 60% of normal, and the market price of rice doubled.

Applying **external criticism** first, **[Source C]** is rejected at once. A document of the mid-eighteenth century that uses twentieth-century chemical-pulp paper, the notation 'CE 1755,' and the words 'proletarian' and 'republic,' which appear only in the late nineteenth century, is clearly a **later forgery**. Sources A, B, and D, on the other hand, are genuine contemporary primary sources.

Next we carry out **internal criticism and cross-verification**. The magistrate's **[Source A]** has a strong motive to minimize and conceal the scale of the peasant protest and the clerks' extortion, which would count against his performance evaluation ('dispersed at once,' 'fairly according to the statutes'). By contrast, when the landlord Kim's **[Source B]** is compared with the accounting ledger **[Source D]**, Source B's statement of 'a further 7 du collected beyond the statutory 14 du per gyeol (21 du in total)' matches exactly the figure in Source D of '21,000 du received from 1,000 gyeol (21 du per gyeol, an excess collection rate of 50%).' Furthermore, applying Braudel's layers of time, we can argue comprehensively that this incident was an **event** (the tax-refusal protest) of the autumn of 1755, but that behind it overlap an **institutional structure**, namely the reform of the taxation system (the Daedongbeop and the gyeoljak of the Gyunyeokbeop) and the passing on of costs to tenants, and a **medium-term conjuncture**, namely worsening Little Ice Age climate, poor harvests, and the soaring price of rice.

examples.title: Quantitative Verification of the Excess Collection Rate (Surcharge Rate) through the Accounting Ledger of Source D
body: Let us compare the total that would have been collected from the 1,000 gyeol of Cheongpo County at the statutory rate (12 du of daedongmi plus 2 du of gyeoljak = 14 du) with the actual amount collected, 21,000 du.

Step 1: The statutory total levy is 1,000 gyeol × 14 du = 14,000 du. Step 2: The excess collected is 21,000 - 14,000 = 7,000 du (7 du per gyeol), and the ratio of excess collection to the statutory amount is (7,000 ÷ 14,000) × 100 = 50%.

Interpretation: The quantitative ledger (Source D) cross-verifies the landlord's diary (Source B) record of 'a further 7 du per gyeol extorted,' and exposes the magistrate's report (Source A) claim of 'fair collection according to the statutes' as a false report.

examples.title: Applying Comparative Insights on East and West Tax Reforms
body: Let us compare the Cheongpo County case (Joseon's Daedongbeop and Gyunyeokbeop) with the Tang Two-Tax Law and the Qing Land-and-Poll-Tax Merger.

Step 1: All three systems tried to shift the tax base from persons (households and adult men) to land area (gyeol, mu), so as to lighten the burden on landless poor peasants. Step 2: But as long as the landlord-tenant system remained, a common structural limit appeared: landlords or clerks passing increases in the land tax on to tenant farmers, or tacking on surcharges (mogok, inju rice).
Interpretation: The success or failure of legal tax reform depended not on the text of the statutes themselves but on the rural power structure and the transparency of tax-collecting administration.

his-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone II: Designing Historical Argument and a Historiographical Critique Essay
explain: The final gateway of the bachelor's program in history is to choose a historical transformation or event of one's own and to **design and write a complete essay of historical argumentation (Historical Argumentation) that combines a source-criticism strategy with historiographical lenses**. A good historical paper is not a mere chronological listing of facts, but work that answers a research question (Research Question) such as 'why and how did such a change occur?' with verifiable sources and a persuasive analytical framework.

A complete essay of historical argumentation is written in the following five-step structure. **(1) Setting the research question and the period and space**: for example, choose one of 'the Gwajeonbeop of late Goryeo to early Joseon and the emergence of the sadaebu,' 'the Tang-Song transition and the shift in the tax system,' 'the contradiction between the declaration of universal human rights and the restriction of suffrage in the Atlantic civic revolutions,' or 'the structural connection between the Industrial Revolution and imperialism.' **(2) Presenting the central thesis (Thesis Statement)**: go beyond linear causal theory and state clearly, in a sentence or two, how structural background and actors' choices combined.

**(3) Arrangement of multiple sources and external and internal criticism**: to support your thesis, state what kinds of sources (official state documents and legal codes, personal collected writings and diaries, quantitative land and price ledgers, material relics, and so on) you will use in cross-reference, and design how you will control, through internal criticism, the biases each source carries (such as the gaze of the ruling class or state).

**(4) Cross-application of historiographical methodologies**: give the event dimension by combining **at least two perspectives** from among Rankean political and institutional history, the longue durée and socioeconomic history of the Annales school (Braudel), the class and history from below of Marxism, the reduced scale and interpretation of symbols of microhistory and the new cultural history, or transnational global history. **(5) Examining counterarguments and the limits of the research**: introduce the strongest alternative interpretation (counterargument) that could be raised against your thesis, rebut it again with source-based evidence, and then honestly state the limits that remain because of gaps in the sources.

After finishing the writing, use the self-check checklist below to verify for yourself whether your essay has both empirical rigor (respect for the veto power of sources) and interpretive depth (a balance of structure and action).

examples.title: An Example of Designing a Historical Argument: The Duality of the Atlantic Civic Revolutions
body: [Research question and thesis] Why did the French Revolution of 1789, after declaring universal natural rights, exclude passive citizens and women from suffrage in the Constitution of 1791? This was a product of a class- and era-bound compromise in which the bourgeoisie, while allying with the common people to break the privileges of the feudal nobility, also sought to defend the order of private property rights.

[Cross-referencing of sources and historiographical lenses] Cross-compare legal sources (the Declaration of Rights and the Constitution of 1791) with Olympe de Gouges's declaration, the petitions of the Paris sans-culottes, and time-series statistics of bread prices. Analyze by combining Marxism and social history (property qualifications and the moral economy) with the new cultural history (discourses of citizenship in the revolutionary period).

[Counterargument and limits] Against the counterargument that 'the revolutionary ideals themselves were hypocrisy from the start,' rebut by pointing to the long-term repercussions: that the very wording of the declaration of universal rights later became a legal and ideological weapon for the Chartist movement, women's suffrage, and the Haitian Revolution.

examples.title: Checkpoints for Controlling Source Bias
body: If you cite only officially compiled sources (the veritable records, Government-General statistics, imperial edicts), it is easy to highlight only the legitimacy of rule or the success of policy.

Be sure to place at least one kind of contrasting source, such as petitions from the harmed classes, local ledgers, oral records, or diplomatic documents of an enemy state, to relativize the recorder's intent.

checks.prompt: What is the most mistaken attitude to avoid when writing an essay of historical argumentation?

checks.explanation: Concealing or distorting counter-evidence that contradicts one's own claim violates the most basic empirical ethic of historical study (the veto power of sources).
options: Quoting only passages favorable to one's thesis, and deliberately hiding contemporary primary sources or quantitative statistics that directly conflict with it
Cross-checking local ledgers or personal diaries to compensate for the state-centered bias of officially compiled sources
Explaining with multiple causes by considering together long-term climate and economic structures and the agentive choices of people of the time
Strictly distinguishing, in the writing, between conjecture and fact for matters that are hard to confirm from the surviving sources alone
